**Given:** The rank-one Coxeter system $W=S_2$, the universal Hecke algebra over its Laurent parameter ring, and the specializations $q=i$, $q=1$, and $q=-1$ over $\mathbb C$.

[F1] [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]]: the rank-one quadratic relation is $(T-v)(T+v^{-1})=0$ for a unit parameter $v$.

[F2] [[thm-hh-generic-coxeter-hecke-standard-basis]]: arbitrary scalar extension presents the specialized Hecke algebra by the images of the same quadratic and braid relations, with no flatness assumption.

[A1] $i^2=-1$, so $i^{-1}=-i$ and $i$ is a unit in $\mathbb C$.

[A2] The values $1$ and $-1$ are units in $\mathbb C$ and each has square $1$.



1.1 For any unit $q$, expanding [F1] and putting $S=qT$ gives $S^2=(q^2-1)S+q^2$, equivalently $(S-q^2)(S+1)=0$; thus the multiplicative source parameter is $\xi=q^2$, while all calculations below keep the local $T$ generator. Now set $q=i$. Then [F1] gives $(T-i)(T+i^{-1})=(T-i)^2=0$, and [F2] identifies this as the complete specialized presentation. With $\epsilon=T-i$, translation $T=\epsilon+i$ gives mutually inverse homomorphisms between $H_2(i)$ and $\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$. Every class has a unique form $a+b\epsilon$: terms of degree at least two vanish, and a polynomial of degree at most one lying in $(\epsilon^2)$ has both coefficients zero. Hence the algebra has basis $1,\epsilon$ and $\epsilon$ is nonzero. [given, F1, F2, A1, algebra, construct]

1.2 For $q=1$ and $q=-1$, [F1] gives the same relation $T^2-1=0$, using [F2] for the specialization. The elements $e_+=(1+T)/2$ and $e_-=(1-T)/2$ are orthogonal idempotents with sum $1$. The classes $1,T$ are linearly independent because no nonzero polynomial of degree at most one is divisible by $T^2-1$, so $e_+$ and $e_-$ are nonzero and form a basis. Thus $H_2(q)=\mathbb C e_+\oplus\mathbb C e_-$, and each one-dimensional left ideal is simple. The regular module is semisimple. [given, F1, F2, A2, algebra, construct]

2.1 The left ideal $\epsilon H_2(i)$ is one-dimensional, nonzero and proper by step 1.1, so the left regular module is not simple. If it were a direct sum of simple left ideals, its dimension two would force it to be a sum of two one-dimensional simple modules. On any one-dimensional module, left multiplication by $\epsilon$ is a scalar $\lambda$ satisfying $\lambda^2=0$, hence $\lambda=0$. It would then annihilate both summands and therefore all of $H_2(i)$, contradicting $\epsilon\cdot1=\epsilon\ne0$. Thus the regular module is not semisimple. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Steps 2.1 and 1.2 establish the two different specialization outcomes under the stated normalized relation. They make no claim about higher ranks, centralizers, positive characteristic, or every root of unity. No choice principle is used: every basis, idempotent, and module complement calculation is explicit and finite. [step 2.1, step 1.2, given] ∎

**Given:** The matrices $R(u)$ and $\check R(u)$ of [[def-hh-rational-spectral-r-matrix]], the identities of [[lem-hh-rational-spectral-r-matrix-satisfies-yang-baxter]], and the braid-group representation interface.

[F1] [[def-hh-rational-spectral-r-matrix]]: $R(u)=uI+iP$ and $\check R(u)=PR(u)$.

[F2] [[lem-hh-rational-spectral-r-matrix-satisfies-yang-baxter]]: for all $x,y,z\in\mathbb C$, both the un-checked and checked spectral equations hold with parameters $x-y$, $x-z$, and $y-z$.

[F3] [[def-yang-baxter-operator-on-an-object]]: a Yang-Baxter operator is an invertible endomorphism satisfying the braid-form equation; invertibility is part of the definition.

[F4] [[thm-a-yang-baxter-operator-gives-braid-group-representations]]: an invertible Yang-Baxter operator gives a homomorphism from each Artin braid group B_n into the automorphism group of the corresponding tensor power.



1.1 The flip $P$ has eigenvalue $1$ on the three-dimensional symmetric subspace, with basis $e_1\otimes e_1$, $e_1\otimes e_2+e_2\otimes e_1$, $e_2\otimes e_2$, and eigenvalue $-1$ on the one-dimensional antisymmetric subspace spanned by $e_1\otimes e_2-e_2\otimes e_1$. Therefore $R(u)=uI+iP$ has eigenvalues $u+i$ and $u-i$ on these two subspaces, while $\check R(u)=uP+iI$ has eigenvalues $u+i$ and $i-u$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 At $u=i$, $R(u)$ vanishes on the antisymmetric line and has rank three; at $u=-i$, it vanishes on the symmetric subspace and has rank one. Thus both $R(u)$ and $\check R(u)$ are invertible exactly away from $u=i$ and $u=-i$. At $u=0$, $R(0)=iP$ and $\check R(0)=iI$ are invertible. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Set $x=i$, $y=0$, $z=0$. Then the checked identity in [F2] has the factors $\check R_1(i)$, $\check R_2(i)$, and $\check R_1(0)$, and both $\check R_1(i)$ and $\check R_2(i)$ are singular by step 2.1. Thus these maps cannot be images of braid-group generators in an automorphism group: the required invertibility in [F3] fails. [given, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 At $u=0$ the checked operator is $iI$. Its local operators on every tensor power are scalar $iI$ and satisfy the Artin braid and distant-commutativity relations; they are invertible because $i$ is nonzero. Thus the assignment $\sigma_j\mapsto iI$ does define a braid-group representation, consistent with [F4]. [given, F1, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The two-auxiliary-leg RTT matrix relation with $R_N(x)=xI+iP_N$.

[F1] [[def-yangian-gl-n-rtt-presentation]]: $R_N(x)=xI+iP_N$ with the auxiliary flip $P_N(e_a\otimes e_b)=e_b\otimes e_a$, and $R_{12}(u-v)T_1(u)T_2(v)=T_2(v)T_1(u)R_{12}(u-v)$.



1.1 In the coefficient of the auxiliary row $(i,k)$ and column $(j,l)$, the $xI$ part of the left side is $x t_{ij}(u)t_{kl}(v)$ and the $iP$ part is $i t_{kj}(u)t_{il}(v)$, because the flip sends the row $(i,k)$ to $(k,i)$. On the right side the corresponding terms are $x t_{kl}(v)t_{ij}(u)$ and $i t_{kj}(v)t_{il}(u)$, since the flip acts on the column. Thus equality of those matrix entries gives $x t_{ij}(u)t_{kl}(v)+i t_{kj}(u)t_{il}(v)=x t_{kl}(v)t_{ij}(u)+i t_{kj}(v)t_{il}(u)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Subtract the two $x$-terms and move the two $i$-terms to the other side. The result is exactly the displayed commutator relation. Conversely, if that relation holds for every four indices, the coefficient computation in step 1.1 makes every auxiliary matrix entry of the RTT difference zero, hence the full matrix relation holds. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** An integer $N\ge2$, the RTT Yangian presentation, and the proposed maps above.

[F1] [[def-yangian-gl-n-rtt-presentation]]: $T_0(u)=I+O(u^{-1})$ satisfies $R_{12}(u-v)T_1(u)T_2(v)=T_2(v)T_1(u)R_{12}(u-v)$, with proposed coproduct matrix product $\Delta(T_0(u))=T_0^{[1]}(u)T_0^{[2]}(u)$, counit $\epsilon(T_0(u))=I$, and antipode formula $S(T_0(u))=T_0(u)^{-1}$.



1.1 Each coefficient of $T^{[1]}(u)T^{[2]}(u)$ is a finite sum: the coefficient of $u^{-n}$ uses only the finitely many pairs of exponents adding to $n$ and the finite index sum $1\le k\le N$. Thus the proposed coproduct lands in the ordinary algebraic tensor product. For two independent Yangian factors, write $T_s^{[r]}$ for the matrix acting on auxiliary leg $s\in\{1,2\}$ and coefficient factor $r\in\{1,2\}$. Then $T_1^{[2]}$ commutes with $T_2^{[1]}$, and $T_1^{[1]}$ commutes with $T_2^{[2]}$, because each pair acts on disjoint tensor factors. Reordering these pairs and applying the RTT relation first in coefficient factor $1$ and then in factor $2$ gives $R_{12}T_1^{[1]}T_1^{[2]}T_2^{[1]}T_2^{[2]}=T_2^{[1]}T_2^{[2]}T_1^{[1]}T_1^{[2]}R_{12}$. The middle matrix product is precisely the RTT relation for $\Delta(T)$, so $\Delta$ preserves the defining relation and extends to a unital algebra homomorphism. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Iterating the matrix product yields $(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(T)=T^{[1]}T^{[2]}T^{[3]}=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\Delta(T)$, so the coproduct is coassociative coefficientwise. Substitution $T\mapsto I$ sends the RTT relation to $R=R$, so it defines a unital counit homomorphism; it also gives $(\epsilon\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(T)=T=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\epsilon)\Delta(T)$ and $\epsilon(1)=1$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Since $T(u)=I+O(u^{-1})$, recursively solving $T(u)T(u)^{-1}=I$ gives a unique right inverse; solving in the reverse order gives a left inverse, and associativity makes them equal. Each inverse coefficient is a finite polynomial in the coefficients of $T-I$, because only products of at most $n$ positive-degree terms contribute to $u^{-n}$. Write $A=T_1(u)$ and $B=T_2(v)$. In $RAB=BAR$, multiply on the left by $A^{-1}B^{-1}=(BA)^{-1}$ and on the right by $B^{-1}A^{-1}=(AB)^{-1}$ to obtain $A^{-1}B^{-1}R=RB^{-1}A^{-1}$. Define an anti-homomorphism on the free generator algebra by sending the coefficient matrix $T(u)$ entrywise to this inverse matrix. Applying it to the defining RTT relator reverses coefficient multiplication, so its image is $R B^{-1}A^{-1}=A^{-1}B^{-1}R$, exactly the same identity. Hence it preserves the RTT ideal and descends to the quotient, with $S(T(u))=T(u)^{-1}$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The two matrix inverse identities give $\sum_k S(t_{ik}(u))t_{kj}(u)=\delta_{ij}=\sum_k t_{ik}(u)S(t_{kj}(u))$, the left and right antipode identities on generators. For the left identity on a product $xy$, use $\Delta(xy)=\sum x_{(1)}y_{(1)}\otimes x_{(2)}y_{(2)}$ and anti-multiplicativity of $S$ to obtain $\sum S(y_{(1)})S(x_{(1)})x_{(2)}y_{(2)}=\epsilon(x)\sum S(y_{(1)})y_{(2)}=\epsilon(x)\epsilon(y)1$; the right identity follows from $\sum x_{(1)}y_{(1)}S(y_{(2)})S(x_{(2)})$. Induction on word length and linearity extend both identities to the generated algebra, giving $m(S\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta=\eta\epsilon=m(\mathrm{id}\otimes S)\Delta$. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** $N\ge2$, the standard basis of $V_N$, and arbitrary $a,b,c\in\mathbb C$.

[F1] [[def-yangian-gl-n-rtt-presentation]]: $P_N(e_j\otimes e_k)=e_k\otimes e_j$, $R_N(x)=xI+iP_N$, and $P_{ij}$ swaps the indicated tensor positions.

[F2] [[def-hh-rational-spectral-r-matrix]]: on the ordered basis of $\mathbb C^2$, $P(e_j\otimes e_k)=e_k\otimes e_j$ and $R(x)=xI+iP$.

[F3] [[lem-hh-rational-spectral-r-matrix-satisfies-yang-baxter]]: for all complex spectral points, the corresponding un-checked three-leg operators satisfy the parameterized Yang–Baxter identity.



1.1 For $N=2$, the ordered basis and flip in [F1] are exactly those in [F2], so $R_2(x)=R(x)$ on the same $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$. The un-checked Yang–Baxter identity for this case is [F3]. [given, F1, F2, F3]

1.2 For $N\ge3$, put $s=P_{12}$, $t=P_{13}$, and $r=P_{23}$. Acting on any basis tensor $e_p\otimes e_q\otimes e_\ell$, the products $st,tr,rs$ all send $(p,q,\ell)$ to $(q,\ell,p)$, while $sr,rt,ts$ all send it to $(\ell,p,q)$; also $str=rts$ as both send $(p,q,\ell)$ to $(\ell,q,p)$. Hence, as operators, with $A=st=tr=rs$ and $B=sr=rt=ts$, those permutation identities hold on the whole basis. [given, F1, algebra]

1.3 The flip satisfies $P_N^2=I$, so direct multiplication gives $(xI+iP_N)(xI-iP_N)=(x^2+1)I=(xI-iP_N)(xI+iP_N)$. Over $\mathbb C$, $x^2+1\ne0$ exactly when $x\notin\{i,-i\}$; division by this scalar gives the stated inverse. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Expanding the left side gives $xyzI+i(yz\,s+xy\,t+xz\,r)-(y\,st+z\,sr+x\,tr)-i\,str$; the right side gives $xyzI+i(yz\,s+xy\,t+xz\,r)-(x\,rt+z\,rs+y\,ts)-i\,rts$. By step 1.2, the quadratic parts are respectively $-((x+y)A+zB)$ and $-(zA+(x+y)B)$, which agree since $x+y=z$; the scalar and linear parts match termwise and the cubic terms match by $str=rts$. This proves the Yang–Baxter identity for all $N\ge3$, and step 1.1 covers $N=2$. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The operators $P_+=(I+P_N)/2$ and $P_-=(I-P_N)/2$ are complementary projectors because $P_N^2=I$. Their images have bases $e_j\otimes e_j$, $e_j\otimes e_k+e_k\otimes e_j$ and $e_j\otimes e_k-e_k\otimes e_j$ for $j<k$, respectively, so their dimensions are $N(N+1)/2$ and $N(N-1)/2$. On these subspaces $R_N(x)$ acts by $x+i$ and $x-i$; therefore at $x=i$ it has kernel $\operatorname{im}P_-=\bigwedge^2V_N$, and at $x=-i$ it has kernel $\operatorname{im}P_+=\operatorname{Sym}^2V_N$, with the ranks stated. [given, F1, step 1.3, algebra] ∎



Each arrow is a composite endomorphism of $V_N^{\otimes3}$, with its rightmost factor applied first. The diagram records the two sides of the equation just proved; the equality follows from the basis-permutation calculation in the proof, not from the diagram.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=huge]
V_N^{\otimes3}
\arrow[r, bend left=35, "R_{12}(x)R_{13}(z)R_{23}(y)"]
\arrow[r, bend right=35, "R_{23}(y)R_{13}(z)R_{12}(x)"']
& V_N^{\otimes3}
\end{tikzcd}
```

**Given:** The RTT presentation for $N=2$, a representation, and a vector satisfying the displayed vacuum eigenvalue conditions.

[F1] [[lem-yangian-rtt-component-commutator-form]]: $x[t_{ij}(u),t_{kl}(v)]=i(t_{kj}(v)t_{il}(u)-t_{kj}(u)t_{il}(v))$ for $x=u-v$.



1.1 Apply [F1] to $(i,j,k,l)=(1,2,1,1)$ and interchange $u,v$; rearranging gives $A(u)B(v)=\frac{x-i}{x}B(v)A(u)+\frac{i}{x}B(u)A(v)$ for $x=u-v\ne0$. Applying [F1] to $(i,j,k,l)=(2,2,1,2)$ gives $D(u)B(v)=\frac{x+i}{x}B(v)D(u)-\frac{i}{x}B(u)D(v)$. All divisions are by the stated nonzero scalar $x$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Apply these identities to $\Omega$ and use its eigenvalue conditions. The coefficient of $B(u)\Omega$ in $(A(u)+D(u))B(v)\Omega$ is $i(a(v)-d(v))/x$, which vanishes under $a(v)=d(v)$. The remaining coefficient of $B(v)\Omega$ is exactly $\Lambda_v(u)$, so the claimed eigenvector identity follows; nonzero-ness of $B(v)\Omega$ makes it an eigenvector rather than merely a zero-vector identity. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** $N\ge2$, $R_i(x)=xI+iP_N$, the RTT relation, and the evaluation-module formula of [[def-yangian-evaluation-module]].

[F1] [[def-yangian-gl-n-rtt-presentation]]: $R_i(x)=xI+iP_N$ and $R_i(u-v)T_1(u)T_2(v)=T_2(v)T_1(u)R_i(u-v)$.

[F2] [[def-yangian-evaluation-module]]: $t_{ij}(u)=\delta_{ij}I-i\rho(E_{ij})/(u-a)$.



1.1 Direct substitution gives $R_i(-i(z-w))=-i((z-w)I-P_N)=-iR_0(z-w)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Substitute $u=-iz$ and $v=-iw$ in the RTT relation [F1]. By step 1.1, each side has the same nonzero scalar factor $-i$, which cancels; the resulting relation is $R_0(z-w)\widetilde T_1(z)\widetilde T_2(w)=\widetilde T_2(w)\widetilde T_1(z)R_0(z-w)$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 In the evaluation module, substitute $u=-iz$ into [F2]. Since $-iz-a=-i(z-ia)$, one obtains $t_{ij}(-iz)=\delta_{ij}I+\rho(E_{ij})/(z-ia)$. Thus the shifted standard evaluation parameter is exactly $ia$. [given, F2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The RTT Yangian of [[def-yangian-gl-n-rtt-presentation]], a $\mathfrak{gl}_N$-module $W$, its action $\rho$, and a spectral shift $a\in\mathbb C$.

[F1] [[def-yangian-gl-n-rtt-presentation]]: $R_N(x)=xI+iP_N$, and the defining relation is $R_{12}(u-v)T_1(u)T_2(v)=T_2(v)T_1(u)R_{12}(u-v)$.

[F2] [[def-yangian-evaluation-module]]: the proposed generator action is $t_{ij}(u)=\delta_{ij}I_W-i\rho(E_{ij})/(u-a)$, and the dual-natural action is $E_{ij}f^k=-\delta_{ik}f^j$.

[F3] [[def-matrix-units]]: $E_{ij}$ is the matrix with entries $(E_{ij})_{rs}=\delta_{ri}\delta_{sj}$.

[F4] [[lem-yangian-rtt-component-commutator-form]]: $x[t_{ij}(u),t_{kl}(v)]=i(t_{kj}(v)t_{il}(u)-t_{kj}(u)t_{il}(v))$ for $x=u-v$ is equivalent to the matrix RTT relation.



1.1 Let $e_1,\ldots,e_N$ be the standard column basis. By [F3], $E_{ij}e_s=\delta_{js}e_i$, so $E_{ij}E_{kl}e_s=\delta_{jk}\delta_{ls}e_i=(\delta_{jk}E_{il})e_s$ for every $s$. Hence $E_{ij}E_{kl}=\delta_{jk}E_{il}$ and $[E_{ij},E_{kl}]=\delta_{jk}E_{il}-\delta_{li}E_{kj}$. On a dual basis vector $f^s$, the explicit commutator is $[\rho^\vee(E_{ij}),\rho^\vee(E_{kl})]f^s=\delta_{ks}\delta_{il}f^j-\delta_{is}\delta_{jk}f^l$. The right side is also $\rho^\vee(\delta_{jk}E_{il}-\delta_{li}E_{kj})f^s$, by the same formula. Thus the dual-natural operators satisfy the matrix-unit bracket and form a $\mathfrak{gl}_N$-representation. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Put $x=u-v$, $U=u-a$, and $V=v-a$. By [F4], the required component identity is the RTT relation to check. Under [F2], its left side is $-x(\delta_{jk}\rho(E_{il})-\delta_{li}\rho(E_{kj}))/(UV)$ by the bracket relation. In the parenthesized difference on the right, the quadratic terms cancel because both are $(-i)^2\rho(E_{kj})\rho(E_{il})/(UV)$. Its linear terms are $-i\delta_{kj}\rho(E_{il})(U^{-1}-V^{-1})-i\delta_{il}\rho(E_{kj})(V^{-1}-U^{-1})=ix(\delta_{jk}\rho(E_{il})-\delta_{li}\rho(E_{kj}))/(UV)$, since $V-U=-x$. Multiplication by the outer factor $i$ therefore gives the same left side. Thus every component RTT relation holds. [given, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The component relations are exactly the coefficients of the matrix relation [F1]. Thus the images of every defining relation vanish, so the assignment on the free generators factors through the RTT quotient and defines the representation $W(a)$. For $W=V_N^\vee$, its auxiliary matrix is $I+iP_N/(u-a)$ by the explicit sum $\sum_{i,j}E_{ij}\otimes E_{ji}=P_N$; multiplying by $u-a$ gives $R_N(u-a)$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The Hopf counit representation, its direct sum on a two-dimensional space, and the one-root Bethe-vector notation from [[lem-yangian-gl2-one-root-bethe-cancellation]].

[F1] [[prop-yangian-gl-n-rtt-hopf-structure]]: $\epsilon(t_{ij}(u))=\delta_{ij}$ defines the counit representation.

[F2] [[lem-yangian-gl2-one-root-bethe-cancellation]]: the one-root condition is $a(v)=d(v)$, and its cancellation theorem assumes the associated Bethe vector is nonzero to conclude it is an eigenvector.



1.1 Let $\mathcal H=\mathbb C e_0\oplus\mathbb C e_1$ be the direct sum of two counit representations and set $\Omega=e_0$. Applying the counit on each summand gives $t_{ij}(u)=\delta_{ij}I_{\mathcal H}$, hence $A=D=I$ and $B=C=0$. Thus the pseudovacuum conditions hold with $a(u)=d(u)=1$, and the one-root equation in [F2] holds for every $v$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 For every $k\ge1$ and parameters $v_1,\ldots,v_k$, the rightmost $B(v_k)$ sends $\Omega$ to zero, so $B(v_1)\cdots B(v_k)\Omega=0$. The empty product is $e_0$. Hence all Bethe vectors from this pseudovacuum span $\mathbb C e_0$, a proper subspace because $e_1$ is linearly independent from $e_0$. Thus the one-root equation by itself does not guarantee completeness. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The Hopf coproduct, the two evaluation modules, and the rational spectral $R$-matrix with its spectral Yang–Baxter equation.

[F1] [[prop-yangian-gl-n-rtt-hopf-structure]]: $\Delta(T(u))=T^{[1]}(u)T^{[2]}(u)$ is a coassociative coproduct; applying the tensor flip to $\Delta$ reverses the two matrix factors.

[F2] [[thm-yangian-evaluation-module-well-defined]]: for any $\mathfrak{gl}_N$-module and parameter $c$, $t_{ij}(u)=\delta_{ij}-i\rho(E_{ij})/(u-c)$ defines a Yangian action; on $V_N^\vee$ its auxiliary Lax matrix is $R_N(u-c)$.

[F3] [[prop-yangian-rational-r-matrix-yang-baxter-and-invertibility]]: $R_{12}(x)R_{13}(x+y)R_{23}(y)=R_{23}(y)R_{13}(x+y)R_{12}(x)$, and $R_N(d)$ is invertible exactly when $d\notin\{i,-i\}$.

[F4] [[def-yangian-evaluation-module]]: $V_N^\vee(a)$ has the dual-natural action and its auxiliary series is $I+iP_N/(u-a)$, whose polynomial Lax matrix is $R_N(u-a)$.



1.1 On the same ordered space $W_a\otimes W_b$, the coproduct action has auxiliary matrix $T_0(u)=T_{0a}(u)T_{0b}(u)$ by [F1]. The opposite coproduct reverses those two matrix factors, giving $T_{0b}(u)T_{0a}(u)$. Multiplying both by the scalar $(u-a)(u-b)$ gives the polynomial products $L_{0a}(u-a)L_{0b}(u-b)$ and $L_{0b}(u-b)L_{0a}(u-a)$, since [F2] and [F4] give $L_{0c}(u-c)=R_{0c}(u-c)$ for $c=a,b$. [given, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 Apply the spectral Yang–Baxter identity [F3] on auxiliary space $0$ and quantum spaces $a,b$, using their indexed-basis identifications and spectral points $u,a,b$. It gives $L_{0a}(u-a)L_{0b}(u-b)R_{ab}(a-b)=R_{ab}(a-b)L_{0b}(u-b)L_{0a}(u-a)$. Since $(u-a)(u-b)$ is nonzero and invertible in the scalar Laurent-series field at infinity, cancel it from the two polynomial Lax products in step 1.1. The resulting identity is the claimed intertwining relation for $T_0(u)$, and equality of its matrix entries gives it for each $t_{ij}(u)$ coefficient. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $a-b\notin\{i,-i\}$, [F3] makes $R_{ab}$ invertible, so the intertwiner is an isomorphism. At $a-b=i$ its kernel is antisymmetric, and at $a-b=-i$ its kernel is symmetric, by [F3]; the identity in step 2.1 still holds because the Yang–Baxter identity is polynomial and no inverse was used. [given, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The finite-dimensional periodic chain, its polynomial monodromy and trace, and the monodromy RTT relation.

[F1] [[def-yangian-periodic-fundamental-chain]]: $\mathcal H$ is finite dimensional, $M_0(u)$ is polynomial in $u$, and $\tau(u)=\operatorname{tr}_0M_0(u)$ is the ordinary auxiliary trace.

[F2] [[lem-yangian-periodic-monodromy-satisfies-rtt]]: $R_{00'}(u-v)M_0(u)M_{0'}(v)=M_{0'}(v)M_0(u)R_{00'}(u-v)$ for every $u,v$.

[F3] [[prop-yangian-rational-r-matrix-yang-baxter-and-invertibility]]: $R_N(d)$ has a two-sided inverse if $d\notin\{i,-i\}$.



1.1 Suppose $u-v\notin\{i,-i\}$. Multiplying the RTT identity [F2] on the right by $R_{00'}(u-v)^{-1}$, which exists by [F3], gives $R_{00'}M_0(u)M_{0'}(v)R_{00'}^{-1}=M_{0'}(v)M_0(u)$. Take the ordinary trace over the two auxiliary spaces. For a finite-dimensional auxiliary matrix $X$ with coefficients in $\operatorname{End}(\mathcal H)$ and an invertible scalar auxiliary matrix $R$, $\operatorname{tr}(RXR^{-1})=\operatorname{tr}(X)$: writing entries, $\sum_{i,j,k}R_{ij}X_{jk}(R^{-1})_{ki}=\sum_{j,k}X_{jk}\sum_i(R^{-1})_{ki}R_{ij}=\sum_jX_{jj}$, since scalar entries commute with the coefficients and $R^{-1}R=I$. Thus the trace of the left side is $\operatorname{tr}_{00'}(M_0(u)M_{0'}(v))$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The tensor-space trace of $M_0(u)M_{0'}(v)$ equals $\tau(u)\tau(v)$, since the two auxiliary factors are independent and the coefficient order is $u$ then $v$. The trace of $M_{0'}(v)M_0(u)$ equals $\tau(v)\tau(u)$ by the same index expansion with the coefficient order reversed. Step 1.1 therefore proves $[\tau(u),\tau(v)]=0$ whenever $u-v\notin\{i,-i\}$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Each matrix entry of $[\tau(u),\tau(v)]$ is a polynomial in $u,v$ by [F1]. For every fixed $v$, it vanishes for all but at most two values of $u$ by step 2.1, hence is the zero polynomial in $u$; consequently it vanishes for all $u,v$. This proves the assertion also at $u-v=\pm i$, where the auxiliary $R$ is singular. [given, F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The two-site chain at $N=2$ with equal inhomogeneities $i/2$, and the transfer-matrix definition and commutativity theorem.

[F1] [[def-yangian-periodic-fundamental-chain]]: $L_{0j}(u)=(u-a_j)I+iP_{0j}$, $M_0(u)=L_{01}(u)L_{02}(u)$, and $\tau(u)=\operatorname{tr}_0M_0(u)$.

[F2] [[thm-yangian-periodic-transfer-matrices-commute]]: the finite periodic chain satisfies $[\tau(u),\tau(v)]=0$ for all complex $u,v$.

[F3] [[def-hh-rational-spectral-r-matrix]]: on the ordered two-dimensional basis, $R(u)=uI+iP$ with $P(e_a\otimes e_b)=e_b\otimes e_a$.



1.1 Set $q=u-i/2$. By [F1] and [F3], $M_0(u)=(qI+iP_{01})(qI+iP_{02})=q^2I+iq(P_{01}+P_{02})-P_{01}P_{02}$. The explicit partial traces are $\operatorname{tr}_0 I=2I$, $\operatorname{tr}_0P_{01}=\operatorname{tr}_0P_{02}=I$, and $\operatorname{tr}_0(P_{01}P_{02})=P_{12}$. For the last identity, expand $P_{0j}=\sum_{r,s}E_{rs}^{(0)}E_{sr}^{(j)}$, multiply using $E_{rs}E_{tu}=\delta_{st}E_{ru}$, and trace the auxiliary factor to obtain $\sum_{r,s}E_{sr}^{(1)}E_{rs}^{(2)}=P_{12}$. Therefore $\tau(u)=2(q^2+iq)I-P_{12}=(2u^2+\tfrac12)I-P_{12}$. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 Substitution $u=i/2$ gives $\tau(i/2)=-P_{12}$, and differentiating the polynomial gives $\tau'(i/2)=4(i/2)I=2iI$. Since $P_{12}^2=I$, the inverse of $-P_{12}$ is $-P_{12}$. Thus $(i/2)\tau'(i/2)\tau(i/2)^{-1}-I=(i/2)(2iI)(-P_{12})-I=P_{12}-I$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The whole polynomial family commutes by [F2], including this specialization; the calculation above identifies one normalized logarithmic derivative and uses no limiting inverse at a singular spectral difference. [given, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
